Fubara lost second-term bid after rejecting political structure that produced him – Wike

content.rendered:
Nyesom Wike, Minister of the Federal Capital Territory (FCT), has said the political crisis that engulfed Rivers State cost Siminalayi Fubara, the governor, the opportunity to seek a second term, blaming the development on what he described as poor advice from political associates and external interests determined to seize control of the state.

Speaking during his monthly media chat aired on Channels Television on Tuesday, Wike said he repeatedly warned Fubara against dismantling the political structure that brought him to power.

“I said, look, don’t derail. Somebody had laid a foundation. Look, this is where I stopped. If you continue this way, our dream is to be able to compete with Lagos. What is wrong with that?” Wike queried.

BusinessDay reports that the rift between Wike and Fubara erupted shortly after Fubara assumed office in 2023, escalating into a prolonged political crisis that culminated in President Bola Tinubu declaring a state of emergency in Rivers in 2025.

Following his reinstatement, Fubara later joined the APC, withdrew from the 2026 governorship primary race, and subsequently endorsed the candidate backed by the Wike-led political family ahead of the 2027 election.

Wike recalled inheriting an administration with virtually no government vehicles and said he rebuilt the Government House and equipped it before leaving office.

According to him, Fubara allowed individuals who opposed his emergence as governor to become his closest advisers, leading him into a needless confrontation with his political benefactors.

“Those who didn’t want you to be governor now became your friends. Obviously, they will destroy you, thinking that coming closer to you is to fight us. At the end of the fight, I have not lost anything. But you have lost. Your intention was to go for a second term, is it not correct? And you are not going,” he said.

Wike maintained that he still harbours no ill feelings towards Fubara.
“If I don’t love him, why would we support him?” he asked.

The FCT minister disclosed that several reconciliation efforts were initiated but collapsed because of political calculations.

“There was a time we all agreed and said, ‘Can we allow bygones to be bygones?’ But something fundamental came up in politics. They said if you allow this now, there are those who want to see that we are no longer politically relevant,” he said.

He further alleged that powerful external interests, including some Senior Advocates of Nigeria, sought to exploit Rivers State for financial gain and encouraged the governor to resist his political camp.

“There are external forces who want to hijack Rivers State. There are those who see Rivers State as a cash cow. We said no, this cash cow must end now,” Wike added.

title.rendered: Super Falcons target WAFCON quarter-final spot against Egypt

content.rendered:
Nigeria’s Super Falcons will be aiming to secure a place in the quarter-finals of the 2026 Women’s Africa Cup of Nations (WAFCON) when they face Egypt in their final Group C match on Wednesday.

The defending African champions head into the decisive encounter knowing victory over Egypt will guarantee their passage to the knockout stage as they continue their quest to retain the continental title and book a place at the next FIFA Women’s World Cup.

Read Also: Super Falcons boost WAFCON title defence with Zambia victory

Falcons bounce back after Malawi setback

Super Falcons recovered impressively from a shock opening defeat to tournament debutants Malawi by edging Zambia 1-0 in their second group game, reviving their hopes of progressing from Group C.

The narrow victory restored confidence within the squad after an unexpected start to the tournament and put Coach Justin Madugu’s side in a strong position ahead of their clash with Egypt.

Despite Egypt’s difficult campaign so far, the Super Falcons are expected to approach the encounter with caution. The North Africans suffered a 6-0 defeat to Zambia in their opening game before falling 3-1 to group leaders Malawi, leaving them rooted at the bottom of the standings.

However, the Nigerian camp insists there will be no complacency, with the coaching staff warning that tournament football often produces surprises.

Madugu forced into selection reshuffle

Super Falcons coach Justin Madugu faces a selection headache after losing two key players to suspension.

Defender Tosin Demehin will miss the match after being sent off for denying Zambia’s Barbra Banda a clear goalscoring opportunity, while midfielder Jennifer Echegini is suspended after accumulating two yellow cards in Nigeria’s opening two fixtures.

The absences are expected to force another tactical reshuffle, with Christy Ucheibe, who impressed in central defence after Demehin’s dismissal against Zambia, likely to partner veteran Osinachi Ohale at the heart of the defence.

In midfield, Toni Payne is tipped to start alongside captain Rasheedat Ajibade, with Halimatu Ayinde also in contention for a place in the starting lineup.

Oshoala, Kanu key to Nigeria’s attack

Madugu is also expected to maintain faith in his attacking options, with Asisat Oshoala and Uchenna Kanu likely to spearhead the Super Falcons’ frontline.

Oshoala scored the decisive goal in the victory over Zambia, while Kanu, who found the net against Malawi, has emerged as another attacking threat.

With a quarter-final berth within reach, the nine-time African champions will be looking to produce another composed display and avoid any slip-up against an Egyptian side desperate to salvage pride from its campaign.

title.rendered: Kaduna targets stronger breastfeeding support as investment in human capital

content.rendered:
The Kaduna State Government has reaffirmed its commitment to expanding breastfeeding and maternal nutrition programmes, describing optimal infant feeding as a strategic investment in human capital capable of improving education outcomes, workforce productivity and long-term socio-economic development.

The commitment was made during the commemoration of World Breastfeeding Week 2026, observed from August 1 to 7 under the theme, “Breastfeeding for a Sustainable Start in Life: Strengthen What Works.”

Addressing journalists on Tuesday at the conference room of Kaduna State Ministry of Health in Kaduna, the Commissioner for Health, Umma Ahmed, said exclusive breastfeeding remains one of the most cost-effective public health interventions for reducing child mortality, combating malnutrition and improving cognitive development, while laying the foundation for a healthier and more productive population.

The commissioner said the state government would continue strengthening maternal, newborn, child and adolescent health services across its 23 local government areas through sustained investments in Infant and Young Child Feeding programmes, Baby-Friendly health facilities, maternal nutrition services, community nutrition initiatives and continuous capacity building for healthcare workers.

She noted that children who receive adequate nutrition during their earliest years are more likely to perform better in school, become economically productive adults and contribute to Kaduna State’s development.

The government also urged families, employers, healthcare providers, traditional and religious leaders, civil society organisations, development partners and the media to create enabling environments that allow mothers to breastfeed successfully.

Mothers were encouraged to initiate breastfeeding within one hour after delivery, practise exclusive breastfeeding for the first six months of life and continue breastfeeding alongside appropriate complementary feeding until two years of age or beyond, in line with national and international health recommendations.

Speaking at the event, Ex-wife Chinese described breastfeeding as one of the strongest foundations for child survival, growth and development, stressing that it extends beyond a health intervention to become a critical investment in human capital.

She said UNICEF and the Kaduna State Government were using this year’s campaign to reinforce the first 1,000 Days Initiative, which focuses on nutrition and child development from conception until a child reaches two years of age.

According to her, this year’s theme shifts attention from creating awareness to strengthening interventions that have already demonstrated measurable impact.

Ezeife commended Kaduna State for adopting six months of paid maternity leave for eligible women, describing the policy as a significant step towards enabling mothers to practise exclusive breastfeeding for the recommended six months.

She also announced the launch of the First 1,000 Days Social and Behaviour Change initiative on nutrition, aimed at encouraging families, workplaces and communities to support breastfeeding beyond the health sector.

She praised the Kaduna State Planning and Budget Commission for establishing workplace crèche facilities and deploying caregivers to enable nursing mothers to continue breastfeeding after returning to work.

The UNICEF nutrition specialist reiterated three evidence-based practices critical to improving child survival: initiating breastfeeding within one hour of birth, practising exclusive breastfeeding for six months without water or other foods, and continuing breastfeeding with complementary feeding until at least two years of age.

She emphasised that maternal nutrition before conception, during pregnancy and throughout breastfeeding directly influences child health outcomes, noting that UNICEF has partnered with the Kaduna State Government to train healthcare workers on Maternal, Infant and Young Child Nutrition to improve counselling and support for mothers.

Ezeife expressed optimism that Kaduna State would record improved breastfeeding indicators beyond those reported in the 2023/2024 Nigeria Demographic and Health Survey, adding that mothers delivering between August 1 and 7 would be monitored to assess early initiation of breastfeeding during the campaign.

She commended the administration of Governor Uba Sani for demonstrating sustained leadership in promoting maternal and child nutrition and called on communities, traditional institutions, religious leaders, local government authorities and healthcare workers to strengthen support systems for nursing mothers.

The event concluded with renewed commitments from government officials, development partners and stakeholders to expand breastfeeding-friendly policies and interventions as part of broader efforts to improve child nutrition, reduce malnutrition and build a healthier future workforce for Kaduna State.

title.rendered: World Bank: AI can fast-track growth in developing economies if governments act now

content.rendered:
Artificial intelligence could help developing economies emerge from their weakest average growth performance in three decades, but only if governments act quickly to address infrastructure and institutional gaps, according to the World Bank Group.

The World Bank’s World Development Report 2026: The Promise of Artificial Intelligence highlights that the technology presents developing nations with an opportunity to achieve in a decade what might otherwise take a century by accelerating economic transformation.

Automation risks lower in developing nations

While global concerns over artificial intelligence have focused on job displacement, the technology is more likely to enhance productivity than replace workers in low- and middle-income countries. The report reveals that only 4,5% of existing jobs in developing economies face automation risk from generative AI, compared with 14,2% in high-income countries.

At the same time, artificial intelligence could significantly boost productivity in 16,2% of jobs across developing economies, closely trailing the 18,7% projected for high-income nations.

“AI has thrown developing economies a lifeline, and they should seize it,” said Indermit Gill, World Bank Group senior vice-president and chief economist.

Gill explained that developing countries do not require massive models or expensive data centres to benefit. Instead, deploying smaller, low-cost tools adapted to local conditions can transform healthcare, education, judicial services, and agricultural extension.

“But they must hurry: AI is spreading faster and is more context-specific than earlier general-purpose technologies like electricity and the internet,” Gill added.

Infrastructure deficits threaten progress

The report marks the institution’s first comprehensive assessment of the technology’s implications for developing regions. Governments and businesses are already deploying systems to solve problems, analyse information, and expand service delivery, particularly where shortages of skilled professionals have constrained progress.

However, the World Bank warned that benefits are far from guaranteed. Many nations lack the electricity, internet access, computing power, local data, and skills required for effective deployment.

“The window to get this right is narrow,” said Gaurav Nayyar, World Development Report 2026 director. “Developing countries that build the foundations now — power, connectivity, skills, and institutions — will be positioned to adopt and adapt AI for their people.”

In Sub-Saharan Africa, nearly one-third of rural schools lack reliable electricity, while more than two-thirds lack dependable internet access. To address these deficits, the World Bank is partnering through Mission 300 to extend electricity access to 300-million people across Sub-Saharan Africa by 2030.

Oyo govt begins house-to-house waste bin enforcement, gives residents one month to comply

content.rendered:
The Oyo State Government has announced the commencement of the enforcement of mandatory waste bin provision for every residential and commercial building across the state, giving residents and property owners one month to comply with the directive, with stringent enforcement effective from September 1st,2026.

The initiative forms part of the State Government’s renewed efforts to strengthen environmental sanitation and ensure proper waste management across Oyo State.

Ademola Aderinto, Commissioner for Environment and Natural Resources, who disclosed this while addressing journalists in his office, explained that every household, residential building, business premises, shopping complex and plaza must provide designated waste bins that are commensurate to the size of the building, the number of occupants and the volume of waste generated.

The Commissioner stressed that all residents and business owners must patronise only government-accredited Private Sector Participants (PSPs) responsible for waste collection and evacuation, warning that anyone found engaging unapproved waste contractors or disposing of waste through unauthorised means would face the full weight of the law.

He urged members of the public experiencing challenges with waste collection services or those uncertain about accredited PSP operators to report to the Oyo State Solid Waste Management Authority (OYOWMA) or the Department of Environmental Health Services of the Ministry of Environment and Natural Resources for necessary guidance and clarification.

Aderinto further revealed that government enforcement teams would also verify evidence of payment of waste evacuation fees during inspections, noting that residents and businesses are expected to remain up to date with their monthly waste disposal payments as part of the requirements for compliance.

The Commissioner explained that the new enforcement exercise is an extension of the state’s daily environmental sanitation initiative, emphasising that having a waste bin and engaging an accredited PSP alone is not sufficient if the surroundings remain dirty.

Judges undersiege: Systemic kidnappings paralyze Nigeria judiciary

content.rendered:
An escalating wave of violent kidnappings targeting High Court and appellate judges across Nigeria has thrown the nation’s legal system into crisis, leaving senior jurists exposed to armed syndicates and terror groups while paralysing court proceedings nationwide.

Heavy weapon-wielding assailants have launched coordinated ambushes on judicial convoys and residential compounds across Kebbi, Borno, Bayelsa, Akwa Ibom, and Edo states. The surge in attacks, driven by multi-million naira ransom demands from North-West criminal syndicates and strategic campaigns by North-East terror groups like ISWAP, has triggered emergency court walkouts and exposed severe deficiencies in federal security infrastructure for the bench.

“An attack on a serving judicial officer is a matter of the utmost gravity,” said Justice Professor Oagile Bethuel Key Dingake of the African Judges and Jurists Forum (AJJF). “The safety and security of judicial officers are indispensable to preserving judicial independence, maintaining public confidence in the justice system, and upholding the rule of law.”

The crisis has spread rapidly from northern border towns to coastal hubs in the Niger Delta, characterised by a lethal trend: highway transit vulnerabilities and immediate, fatal violence directed at police escorts.

In Kebbi State, on July 26, 2026, Justice Faruku Hassan Bunza of the Kebbi State High Court was dragged from his residence by armed bandits shortly after returning from official business. Denouncing the abduction, Nigerian Bar Association (NBA) President Afam Osigwe, SAN, called the incident “a dangerous challenge to the administration of justice” that “raises fresh concerns over the safety of judicial officers across the country.”

In a deadly terror-linked attack in Borno State on June 24, 2024, Justice Haruna Mshelia of the Borno State High Court, along with his wife, driver, and police orderly, was ambushed along the volatile Biu-Maiduguri highway by suspected ISWAP insurgents operating near the Sambisa Forest border. Meanwhile, in Bayelsa State, on June 21, 2025, Justice Ebiyerin Omukoro was seized outside a commercial establishment in Yenagoa by masked gunmen in broad daylight. Nigerian Law Society (NLS) President Mela Nunghe, SAN, labelled the act a “gross violation of the Nigerian Constitution,” emphasising that judge security is essential to maintaining public trust.

Convoy ambushes in Akwa Ibom and Edo states have repeatedly overwhelmed security details. In Akwa Ibom, Justice Joy Uwanna was abducted on December 18, 2023, after attackers executed her police orderly on the road. A similar fate befell the security detail of Appeal Court Justice Chioma Nwosu-Iheme during her abduction on October 30, 2019, in Edo State, underscoring that standard police escorts are regularly outgunned. Following Justice Uwanna’s abduction, the Akwa Ibom State Police Command released a statement conceding the severity of the situation: “It’s very unfortunate that a judge who presides over high court has been kidnapped… No stone will be left unturned, resources will be harnessed to ensure that Her Lordship is reunited with her family.”

While financial gain drives banditry in the North-West and Niger Delta, the strategic targeting of jurists threatens to dismantle the administration of justice entirely. Armed groups consistently outgun assigned security orderlies both in transit and inside secure compounds, rendering traditional protection protocols ineffective.

In response to the targeted violence, judicial associations in several affected states have staged strikes and court walkouts. Bar leadership and bench members are demanding immediate federal interventions, including high-level specialised security details and armoured transport vehicles for judges travelling high-risk routes. As courtrooms sit empty across the country, the Nigerian judiciary faces an existential question: how to dispense justice in a security landscape where judicial robes provide no shelter against armed violence.
